summary: Chin Keong Lam, founder and CEO of Patho AI, shares lessons learned building expert AI systems for large corporate clients. Patho AI originated two years ago from an NSF SBIR grant investigating LLM-driven drug discovery, and has since expanded to building AI systems that perform research and advisory roles beyond traditional RAG. Lam defines knowledge as understanding gained through experience and education, and knowledge graphs as a systematic method of preserving wisdom by connecting information into networks of interrelated relationships that represent the thought process and comprehensive taxonomy of a specific domain. He introduces KAG (Knowledge Augmented Generation) as distinct from RAG—KAG integrates structured knowledge graphs to enable AI that doesn't just retrieve information but understands and reasons about it. The core framework is the Wisdom-Decision Making-Situation state diagram. Wisdom is the central node that actively guides decision making. Decisions analyze real-world situations. The diagram includes feedback loops: knowledge feeds wisdom, situations inform future wisdom, and experience deepens insight. Lam uses a pizza analogy: knowledge is the recipe, experience is knowing your oven burns the crust, and insight is discovering that adding honey caramelizes it. For practical application, Lam describes a competitive analysis chatbot built for a client. The system maps the wisdom taxonomy to specific components: wisdom maps to a wisdom engine (orchestration agent), decision making maps to a strategy generator, knowledge maps to market data, experience maps to past campaigns, insight maps to industry insights, and situation maps to product performance and competitor weaknesses. Implementation uses N8n, a no-code workflow automation tool with Node.js underneath. Lam maps the state diagram to a multi-agent system where a wisdom agent acts as supervisory agent over specialized agents such as an insight agent that monitors social media sentiment. All agents update a centralized knowledge graph containing the unified taxonomy. Lam argues knowledge graphs excel over vector RAG for five reasons: capturing complex relationships for deeper contextual understanding, improving accuracy through structured data and semantic relationships, offering scalability and flexibility for continuous improvement, rich query capabilities for multihop questions, and enhanced data integration across diverse sources. He highlights that vector RAG struggles with numerical reasoning—returning passages instead of precise figures—while knowledge graphs enable evidence-based decision making with exact quantitative answers. Lam recommends a hybrid approach for building KAG systems: simple chroma DB with LLM agents for basic product queries, and knowledge graphs with graph DB plus Cypher queries and multihop loops for complex strategic questions. For graph extraction, he recommends a hybrid model combining automated LLM graph transformers with expert review to prune the graph and refine the taxonomy. Benchmark results show 91% accuracy, 85% flexibility, plus reproducibility, traceability, and scalability. He concludes that wisdom-driven KAG can potentially surpass the intelligence of the initial expert it was meant to serve, and shares an open-source LLM graph RAG stack on GitHub sponsored by Neo4j.

sections.title: Introduction to Patho AI and KAG
sections.summary: Lam introduces himself as founder and CEO of Patho AI, which started two years ago with an NSF SBIR grant for LLM-driven drug discovery and now builds expert AI systems for large corporate clients that go beyond RAG, performing research and advisory roles.

sections.title: Defining Knowledge and Knowledge Graphs
sections.summary: Lam defines knowledge philosophically as understanding gained through experience and education, and knowledge graphs as a systematic method of preserving wisdom by connecting relationships into a network representing the thought process and taxonomy of a domain.

sections.title: KAG vs RAG
sections.summary: KAG (Knowledge Augmented Generation) is introduced as different from RAG, enhancing language models by integrating structured knowledge graphs for more accurate and insightful responses. KAG doesn't just retrieve—it understands.

sections.title: The Wisdom-Decision Making-Situation Diagram
sections.summary: Lam presents a state diagram with wisdom as the core node actively guiding decision making, which analyzes real-world situations. Feedback loops connect knowledge to wisdom, insight to wisdom, and situation to wisdom. Uses a pizza analogy and emphasizes wisdom as a muscle exercised through feedback, not a static trophy.

sections.title: Practical Application: Competitive Analysis Chatbot
sections.summary: Lam describes a competitive analysis chatbot built for a client, mapping the wisdom taxonomy to system components: wisdom engine as orchestration agent, strategy generator for decision making, market data for knowledge, past campaigns for experience, industry insights for insight, and competitor weaknesses for situation.

sections.title: Implementation with N8n and Multi-Agent System
sections.summary: Lam explains using N8n for prototyping the multi-agent system. A wisdom agent acts as supervisory agent over specialized agents, with all agents updating a centralized knowledge graph. The wisdom agent can drive different models (OpenAI, Anthropic, on-prem). The unified knowledge graph contains the taxonomy for decision-making.

sections.title: Why Use Knowledge Graphs over RAG
sections.summary: Lam argues knowledge graphs outperform vector RAG for five reasons: capturing complex relationships for deeper contextual understanding, improving accuracy through structured data and semantic relationships, offering scalability and flexibility, rich query capabilities for multihop questions, and enhanced data integration across diverse sources including pictures, graphics, and videos.

sections.title: Challenges with Vector RAG and Numerical Reasoning
sections.summary: Lam explains vector RAG is bad at numerical reasoning, returning passages instead of precise figures. Knowledge graphs store data in structured form enabling exact quantitative answers. Example: Apple revenue query returns 15.23% growth figure via function call rather than retrieved passages, enabling evidence-based decision making.

sections.title: Building KAG Systems and Hybrid Models
sections.summary: Lam presents a hybrid architecture: simple chroma DB with LLM agents for basic product queries, and knowledge graphs with graph DB plus Cypher queries and multihop loops for complex strategic questions like beating competition based on market share. LangChain plus Chroma can combine with knowledge graphs depending on use case.

sections.title: Graph Extraction and Benchmarks
sections.summary: Lam recommends hybrid graph extraction: automated LLM graph transformers combined with expert review to prune the graph and refine taxonomy. Benchmark results show 91% accuracy, 85% flexibility, reproducibility, traceability, and scalability as key metrics favoring knowledge graph KAG.

sections.title: Conclusion and Resources
sections.summary: Lam concludes that wisdom-driven KAG significantly enhances quantitative capabilities and can potentially surpass the intelligence of the initial expert it was built to serve. He shares an open-source LLM graph RAG stack on GitHub sponsored by Neo4j that spins up via Docker for rapid graph extraction and pruning.
